vignette: It begins on a Tuesday evening at a cramped neighborhood café where Elias plays a twelve-piece set for a handful of regulars. After his final chord fades, a woman approaches the stage. She says she has been listening to his recordings for years, her voice steady, her eyes fixed. He smiles, exchanges his usual polite thanks, and steps into the cool night air. Within weeks, her presence multiplies. Notes slip into the lining of his acoustic guitar. His phone fills with voicemails that disconnect before he can press play. He tells himself it is harmless attention, but the fear settles in his chest like a heavy stone. He changes his route home. He avoids the venues he has played for a decade. He tells his then-wife that it is a passing nuisance, though the dread does not pass. The harassment tightens its grip. Someone begins standing close behind him in grocery aisles, close enough that he can smell citrus and cigarette smoke over the sweat gathering at his collar. He recognizes a black sedan in three different districts. He buys a security camera, prints out screenshots, files police reports. The folders multiply on his desk while his sleep thins to glass. He dreams of stage monitors turning into staring eyes, of locked doors that slide open in the dark, of hands reaching through speaker grilles to tune his ribs. His father's generation taught him to swallow the heat of shame, to keep the family name quiet and dignified, so he says nothing to his parents. He tells his wife he can handle it. She tells him he cannot, and asks him to leave the apartment because the constant scanning of exits and the exhaustion in his eyes have made their home feel like a waiting room. He packs his instrument cases and moves to a ground-floor unit with deadbolts on every door. Now, at fifty, Elias lives in a coastal town where the rain falls often and the streets stay empty. He makes a modest living tuning strings and repairing broken bridges for conservatory students, work that rewards patience and stillness. His hands, once celebrated for flying across fretboards during live sets, now move with careful precision over rusted tuning pegs and frayed windings. He misses the music. He misses the way an audience would lean into the quiet passages, how the air would hold its breath. But the thought of stepping onto a stage makes his shoulders hike toward his ears and his breath shorten. He imagines the crowd as a single face, the darkness as a blind spot, the silence as a held breath before a word he has not heard yet. He drinks his tea quickly and walks to work through back alleys, head down, listening for footsteps that match his own. He does not speak of her much in our sessions. When he does, his voice stays level, but his thumb traces the worn wood of his chair arm, counting the grooves. He describes the exhaustion of being perpetually awake inside his own skin, the way trust feels like a door left ajar, the way the silence between his ribs is never really empty. He knows the police file is closed. He knows the dates have passed. He knows he should let the music breathe again. Some evenings, he sets his guitar on its stand, turns it toward the window, and waits for dawn the way he always has, waiting for the world to stop holding its breath.
